## Introduction - An Intersection Between Data Science and Humanities

Throughout history eagles have appeared all over coinage. The earliest Greeks and Romans minted the bird somewhat randomly, but over time it grew to have clear symbolic meaning. Or more accurately, it meant a number of very different things to almost every person depending solely on where and when they came from. But despite how varied its meaning was (and still is), it persevered through the Roman imperial period, and is a very common piece of iconography on the coins of numerous modern countries.

Take for example two ancient eagles and two modern eagles:

The eagle was an incredibly common symbol on both Ptolemaic Imperial and Roman Imperial coinage, but their meanings were starkly different. On early Ptolemaic coinage, the eagle represented a divine authority and connection to Alexander the Great, while on the Roman Imperial coins it served as a symbol of Roman virtues. Despite that, these eagles are markedly similar in design.

::: {layout-ncol="2"}

![A coin of the late Ptolemaic empire](images/other images/PTcoin1.jpg)

![A coin of the Roman empire just following Augustus' death](images/other images/TBcoin1.jpg)

:::

Likewise in the (relatively) modern day, the eagle on Mexican pesos can be interpreted as representative of the historical myth of Mexico's founding, while on American coins it typically represents liberty, freedom, and general patriotic symbolism.

## The Project

As this project grew in scope a number of new goals arose for me, on top of those I originally pursued. In order to chase those new ideas, though, I needed to commit a substantial amount of time to not only learning but applying skills as a data analyst.

During my first few days in Germany I built a roadmap with goals for the trip. I went on to complete all of these goals, despite the fact that I constantly changed ideas or added new ones to the list as the trip progressed. My goals were as follows:

1.  Build a dataset from the coins I see that feature eagles.

2.  Learn about the cataloging process of ancient coins and how it differs between different collections, as well as study how different collections and museums present their coins — then, write about the positives and negatives that come with different methods.

3.  Train an image classification model to discern coins with eagles from coins without eagles.

4.  Develop a price prediction model for ancient coins via linear regression and historical auction data.

5.  Launch a website to display everything I develop: My datasets and their analysis, maps of eagle coin mintings throughout history, the models I've built, and what I learn about cataloging, sourcing, and presentation of coins through collections and museums.

The launch of this website marks my final objective complete. At this point all of the other goals on the list are complete and can be found/interacted with in different pages on this site. It's important to note, though, that each of these overarching goals was secretly a number of smaller objectives, so even the seemingly simple ones required a number of different skills and steps to complete.

Along with my analysis, the datasets I built/sourced can be found throughout the website's pages, free for you to scroll through if so desired. If something seems missing that you wish you could access, the github repo for this site is linked in the upper bar of every page and is publicly accessible, so please feel free to look through it.
